questions.q: In a constant-product pool holding 100 ETH and 200,000 USDC, what is the invariant k?
questions.explain: k = x * y = 100 * 200,000 = 20,000,000, and every trade must keep this product constant (or growing from fees).

questions.q: After a trader sends 10 ETH into the 100 ETH / 200,000 USDC pool, approximately how much USDC do they receive?
questions.explain: New y = k / 110 = 181,818.18, so USDC out = 200,000 - 181,818.18 = 18,181.82 — less than the naive 10 * 2,000 = 20,000 due to price impact.

questions.q: What causes "price impact" in a constant-product AMM?
options: A separate fee the protocol charges on top of the trade
An arbitrary price the protocol team sets each day
A direct, mechanical consequence of the x*y=k formula as reserves shift during the trade
A tax imposed by the blockchain network itself
questions.explain: Price impact comes straight from the formula: as the trade changes the reserve ratio, the effective price paid moves away from the pre-trade spot price.

questions.q: Why does a 50 ETH trade move the price far more (in percentage terms) than a 1 ETH trade in the same pool?
options: Because larger trades are charged a higher percentage fee by the protocol
Because the pool resets its reserves between large trades
There is no actual difference in price impact between trade sizes
Because the x*y=k curve is a hyperbola that steepens as a reserve is depleted, so larger trades face disproportionately worse pricing
questions.explain: The worked table shows price impact growing from about -1% at 1 ETH to over -33% at 50 ETH — a direct result of the curve's shape, not a fee schedule.

questions.q: What determines how much price impact a given trade size produces, more than anything a protocol team can tune?
options: Pool depth — how large the reserves are relative to the trade size
The color scheme of the protocol's front-end
The number of validators on the blockchain
The trader's wallet balance in other tokens
questions.explain: Deeper pools (larger reserves relative to trade size) produce smaller price impact; this is a structural property of the reserves, not a configurable setting.
